title: After 7 months, Glasswing overwelms maintainers with underwhelming findings (vulncheck.com)
comments: I received 9 reports of Fil-C issues from AnthropicAll of them were real bugs. None of them were false positives.The quality of the reports was exceptional. (My baseline is doing security defense on a browser engine, so my baseline has a large sample count and is probably representative of what experts are capable of.)The quality of the proposed fixes was alright. I took some of the fixes verbatim. I used most of the fixes as significant inspiration for doing it my way.The quality of the test cases was exceptional.Maybe I’m special somehow! But I just want to call out the enormous chasm between what I saw of anthropic’s capability and what TFA saysreply

A simple reason could be the age of the codebase. New code contains more serious bugs, and younger projects are made up of more new code than more mature projects. In older code, especially well-used older code, many serious issues have already been found and fixed.reply

It’s not a reason for the wide chasm though.If you told me that some significant number of Ant findings were duds, then I could reconcile that with what I saw first hand.But TFA is making a more extreme statementreply
The reason is that's just how AI is. It has a very jagged edge of experience. In some ways it's bizarrely wrong and in some ways it seems like a mystical crystal ball.reply
Likely difference between individual experience and group experience.Useful to figure out if there are other cases like yours, so then commonalities can be inferred.reply
TotallyI’m just sharing my data pointreply

That's interesting. While the curl maintainer seems to have been underwhelmed with Mythos 5 in particular, it looks like he also backs up your account of high-quality AI reports (although unclear if these come from Glasswing or elsewhere) at this point.> The slop is gone> A sizeable portion of users seem to still believe we still suffer from a lot of made up and hallucinated reports by these AIs. We really don’t.> Almost all the stupidity and lies we saw in the vulnerability reports made by AIs in the past have ceased. Since spring 2026 the slop reports are practically gone. Our current challenge is much harder: high volume, high quality.https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2026/10/22/ignore-the-slop/reply

Linux maintainer is extremely unhappy with the high false positive rate from Mythos vuln: https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=NnV_cWeoo5Q&pp=0gcJCVgCo7VqN5t...I think someone who likes AI thinks it’s good, someone who doesn’t, doesn’t think it’s anything impressive, and concretely nothing of any significance has happened to the world, certainly nothing like the crowdstrike shutdown so I don’t find the capabilities to be anything impressive.reply

> and concretely nothing of any significance has happened to the worldI would hypothesize that all the long-held "easily discovered if you look in the right place, but never reported and so never fixed" 0days in operating systems that criminal gangs and militaries have been relying on (to do cyberattacks with, unlock devices for forensic data recovery with, etc.), are increasingly being exposed and cleaned up, much faster than new such exploits can be discovered; and that this may have given an edge to whichever side of these conflicts don't rely so heavily on hacking the other to achieve their goals.reply

> Linux maintainerI wonder what it's like maintaining a project where you regularly get competent contributions. No wonder they are less impressed with AI - they are the 0.1% of maintainers who had something better.reply

title: Scion is back and is going to sell a kei truck in America (theautopian.com)
comments: I use a kei truck for farming. They are incredibly pragmatic little vehicles. They are very capable driving around on dirt/gravel agricultural roads with 4WD, and they are inexpensive and robust enough that you can really beat them up and use them as a tool without worry. Repairs and replacement parts are ubiquitous and inexpensive. Having the sides of bed fold down is also really useful.They aren't comfortable to drive at all (although just having A/C at all on a hot summer day in the field is a godsend), and I wouldn't want to do longer trips in one - although you certainly could in a pinch.It seems like Toyota/Scion is just testing the waters here, and I'm not sure how successful they'll be. But I hope there is a future for kei trucks in the US.reply

I've been driving a 2 seater manual Ford Ranger for the past 15 years and it definitely feels like the next level up of the kei philosophy. I'll probably drive it for the rest of my life at this point. It has crank windows, it's indestructible, and it climbs stuff like a little buggy - I've taken it places where sometimes even Jeeps struggle. It's not the car you take on a long road trip, but maybe different tools for different jobs.It's a shame they don't really make them anymore. If I could buy a modern vehicle in the States that had the following properties:- 2 seater- Pickup truck- Manual transmission- Minimum 6 foot bedI'd probably do it in a heartbeat. But even these somewhat weak constraints fail every vehicle in the USA market.reply

> - Manual transmissionThe Toyota eCVT is an engineering marvel[1].The hybrid power train is simpler than a regular transmission and made of more durable parts.The clutch itself might not have to disappear for more fine grained power delivery, the new Ferrari clutch-by-wire[2] is a similar bit of a few hall sensors talking to the ECU.You can build a simulacrum of a manual low-mode transmission without needing to use it constantly in stop-go traffic or while sliding backwards on loose dirt.[1] - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r2L5VOtf47Y[2] - https://www.ferrari.com/en-EN/corporate/articles/ferrari-12c...reply

In kei trucks I think the manual transmission is mainly just about cost of ownership. A new 4WD kei truck with MT costs ¥1,226,500 ($7,727 USD) compared to ¥1,303,500 ($8,212) for an automatic transmission - about 6% less [1]. And longer term repairs/replacement of a manual transmission tend to be less costly than an automatic transmission. Not a huge difference - but the applications where these trucks tend to be used are not exactly high margin, either.I don't think we're likely to see a Toyota hybrid system or Ferarri-style drive-by-wire clutch at that price point. Although maybe in the future we could see EV kei trucks at a comparable price [2].Personally I think it's worth spending slightly more for the convenience of a manual transmission (and my license doesn't actually permit me to drive a manual on public roads) - although some of my buddies laughed at me for buying an automatic kei truck. I think at this point though automatic transmission sales probably exceed manual transmission sales.[1] https://www.daihatsu.co.jp/lineup/truck/02_grade.htm?item=6[2] https://electrek.co/2026/11/01/i-imported-a-2000-electric-tr...reply

I always found it interesting that Europe and other international locales separate manual vs automatic in license grades. The USA does not - my license does not care if the car I operate is manual or automatic. I'm classed based on weight and axles and length only.On one hand, you would think it makes sense. It IS an additional skillset to operate a manual transmission vehicle. On the other hand, if you can't operate a manual properly, you aren't getting very far anyway. Was there really that big of a spate of "I didn't know how to operate the manual, so I wrecked the vehicle" sort of issues in Europe and elsewhere that pre-empt this and justify the extra bureaucracy?reply

Japan is a lot stricter than the US when it comes to driving in general. The minimum age is higher, the driving test is more difficult, it's easier to lose your license for traffic violations, speed limits are lower, mandated vehicle inspections are much more expensive/comprehensive, there is zero tolerance for drinking and driving (even one sip), etc. This is reflected in traffic fatality figures - 12.8 deaths per 100,000 people in the US vs 1.9 in Japan [1].So while I'm not sure about the origin of manual vs automatic licenses specifically, it's not really surprising in the broader context of Japan's strict stance on driving.In practice it means if you want to drive manual, you need to take the driving test in a manual - which is not unreasonable. But seeing as how only 13% of foreigners pass Japan's practical driving test on the first attempt (to be fair, it was easier back when I took it) [2], and I hadn't driven manual in years, I wasn't looking to make things any more difficult for myself.Or there is also the option to take some lessons at a driving school and get certified to drive a manual (with the assessment at the end being easier than taking the official test). But I haven't really had a good reason to bother with this.[1] https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/death-rates-road-incident...[2] https://www.asahi.com/ajw/articles/16392895reply

Ford more or less uses the same eCVT in the Maverick. They are the best hybrid transmission by far, but they still require a generator and high voltage battery.For dirt-simple, low-fi reliability a manual transmission is still the guy for the job. I generally buy older cars and I almost never buy a car over 150k miles unless is has an manual.reply

> they still require a generator and high voltage battery.They require two generators, but they also don't require a starter motor or an alternator. Meanwhile a non-plugin hybrid only needs around 2 kWh worth of battery, which has gotten so cheap you might prefer that to a clutch replacement.reply

title: .name Grandfathered (neil.fraser.name)
comments: > After a long and expensive battle, news just dropped that Verisign is retracting its plan to terminate 22,000 domain names and email redirects. Although they will be closing new registrations for 3rd-level .name domains, all existing domains (including this website) and email redirects will remain indefinitely.This was what I figured SHOULD happen when they did this. Allow existing customers to keep renewing, but nobody new allowed, if a tld frees up over time, reclaim it completely and sell it off.What they were proposing should really be illegal...reply

For it to be illegal I think we would have to have much stronger digital ownership laws. I would certainly support them. But for now a domain you "own" is just an entry in someone else's ledger and control is only enforced by contract for big players willing to pay.reply

There is a Ninth Circuit decision that domain names are a form of propertyhttps://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kremen_v._Cohenbut it's tricky because the domain name registries and registrars have a kind of thicket of contracts nowadays that subordinates registrants' property interests to other rules and considerations. So I don't think a court would think that a modern-day domain name registrant has property rights in a domain name that supersede all of those contractual terms.Edit: my recollection is that Kremen v. Cohen interpreted the legal defaults that applied because Kremen registered the domain name in an era when Network Solutions didn't require registrants to agree to a contract that limited Network Solutions's liability and gave it various explicit rights and powers.I'm not a huge ICANN expert, but I think ICANN broadly thinks the status quo is preferable to one in which registrants had stronger, less equivocal property interests in names.reply

The Wikipedia summary of the case suggests that the ruling was much more than it was. Courts tend to rule on narrow issues, as it did here.The question before the Court was not whether a domain name is a form of property. Both parties agreed that a domain name is a form of property; that wasn't in dispute. The Court did affirm their shared position in black letter law, though.Rather, the question before the Court was whether, as intangible property, a tort of conversion claim relating to the domain name could be made under California law. Previously, cases disagreed as to whether it could be recognized. The Court found that it could be.reply
Thanks. That was an excellent summary.reply
Agreed, but I just wanted to say that essentially every single thing anyone owns is, and has been from the invention of tally marks on clay tablets, an entry in someone's ledger.reply

This is too reductive. There's been real development behind what it means to own something. What's written in a ledger is just an inscription it has no meaning outside of its social context.Our social understanding of property has changed. John Locke's ideas on private property are so fundamental to how we think about ownership that we don't even realize there would have been another way of thinking about how we own things.https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_property#Historyreply
Of all the thousands of things I own, as far as I know, only my car and my house exist in anyone else's ledger as belonging to me. Am I missing something?reply

I would find that hard to believe. You have a bank account, surely. A life insurance policy? Airline points? An account with the government social security office for your pension? There are probably dozens (if not hundreds) of things of value (even if the value is near zero) that exist in someone else's ledger.reply
All of your property exists in a kind of implicit ledger that a court can reify when needed. If a court decides your bed isn't yours, then it isn't.reply

title: Smart home devices should work without the internet (docodethatmatters.com)
comments: Bought our home almost 20 years ago, and the former owner (apparently) owned a now-defunct home automation business. The upside was 100% X10/Insteon power and light controls, top alarm panel, environmental controls and so on running off of a wall-mounted "SmartLinc" touch panel. I expanded the system with Axis cameras and a Mac Server running Indigo and SecuritySpy (non-subscription), which enabled remote monitoring and control, but it all operates locally.In a moment of weakness, I bought a D-Link wireless (wifi) water detector for the sump pit (it was on clearance for $30); it relied on a D-Link Home cloud service (free) that was closed down a few years ago.Not wanting to toss it, I repurposed a spare Chromebook 14 that I was going to recycle and turned it into a Alpine monitor for the water detector, which I'm powering from the Chromebook's USB port (if power is lost in a rainstorm, I need to know about it before the sump pit fills up).An immediate issue was that the D-Link firmware tried to "phone home" every 24 hours and would drop from the local network, since the server was kaput, and I had no clue what response it was expecting from the server to keep it alive. Solution; "reboot" the unit by interrupting USB power (with a Pico and MOSFET) every 23 hours. There's no question that home automation should work without the internet.reply

> Solution; "reboot" the unit by interrupting USB power (with a Pico and MOSFET) every 23 hoursReminds me of a possible apocryphal anecdote I heard about Alan Turing.  He loved going on long bike rides, but one day his bike developed a distressing habit of slipping the chain.  After the third time it happened, he realized it was due to a broken tooth on both the front and the back gear.  He went back home and calculated how many revolutions of the pedals it would take for both broken teeth to line up when they were at the critical part of the rotation, and he built a little mechanical counter that would click on each link in the bike chain, and at the calculated time, a little arm would reach down and clasp the chain, holding it in place long enough for the teeth to re-engage.He showed the device to his friend, who said "Why didn't you just buy new gears?  You could have gotten both for a dime."  And Alan replied "Oh, that's clever, I didn't think of that."reply

Somewhat related [1]:> Years ago, I was working at Video Seven, a now-vanished video adapter manufacturer, helping to develop a VGA clone. The fellow who was designing Video Seven’s VGA chip, Tom Wilson, had worked around the clock for months to make his VGA run as fast as possible, and was confident he had pretty much maxed out its performance. As Tom was putting the finishing touches on his chip design, however, news came fourth-hand that a competitor, Paradise, had juiced up the performance of the clone they were developing by putting in a FIFO.> That was all he knew; there was no information about what sort of FIFO, or how much it helped, or anything else. Nonetheless, Tom, normally an affable, laid-back sort, took on the wide-awake, haunted look of a man with too much caffeine in him and no answers to show for it, as he tried to figure out, from hopelessly thin information, what Paradise had done. Finally, he concluded that Paradise must have put a write FIFO between the system bus and the VGA, so that when the CPU wrote to video memory, the write immediately went into the FIFO, allowing the CPU to keep on processing instead of stalling each time it wrote to display memory.> Tom couldn’t spare the gates or the time to do a full FIFO, but he could implement a one-deep FIFO, allowing the CPU to get one write ahead of the VGA. He wasn’t sure how well it would work, but it was all he could do, so he put it in and taped out the chip.> The one-deep FIFO turned out to work astonishingly well; for a time, Video Seven’s VGAs were the fastest around, a testament to Tom’s ingenuity and creativity under pressure. However, the truly remarkable part of this story is that Paradise’s FIFO design turned out to bear not the slightest resemblance to Tom’s, and didn’t work as well. Paradise had stuck a read FIFO between display memory and the video output stage of the VGA, allowing the video output to read ahead, so that when the CPU wanted to access display memory, pixels could come from the FIFO while the CPU was serviced immediately. That did indeed help performance—but not as much as Tom’s write FIFO.[1] https://www.jagregory.com/abrash-black-book/#the-challenge-o...reply

The clever 6809 PSHU/PULS memory copy trick was probably independently discovered several times before Tom Moertel discovered it. The game Tom worked on was for the Coco 3, which was released in 1986.My first computer was the original 4K Color Computer (1981). I learned 6809 assembler on it and worked full time programming it for several years, while also running one of the largest users groups for it. Traveling to Coco trade shows around the country, I met many of the devs writing the most popular Coco games and the trick was definitely known by around Summer 1983 as that's when the first Rainbowfest was held and I heard about there.Around 1983, Steve Bjork (MegaBug / Zaxxon Coco) told me the devs at DataSoft, the company behind some of the popular 1st party cartridge games Radio Shack sold, were using it. I also heard about it in 1984 from Tim Jenison (CocoMax).The earliest known usage in a released game was probably in a Williams arcade game like Defender (1981) or Joust (1982). A few years ago at the Hackers Conference Tim told me he'd once asked Eugene Jarvis (Joust, Defender) if he knew the trick and Eugene told him they'd used in a few Williams game and nicknamed the trick "PUSH-U / PUL-Me." I confirmed this with Sam Dicker (Sinistar, Defender) last year at the Amiga 040th anniversary at the Computer History Museum.While the basic trick to do a fast software block image transfer discovered by a lot of 6809 programmers, until today I can't recall ever seeing the Direct Page (DP) register used with it before today. That and some of the other refinements are quite clever additions. I think the Coco's lack of any hardware sprites, tiles, scrolling or acceleration made Coco devs especially desperate, so we had to become masters of software blits with PSHU/PULS and software sprites with XOR.reply

I started programming by making games in TI-BASIC, for the TI-83+ graphing calculators. There were some weird tricks like omitting all ending parentheses. Good preparation for weird hacks in real languages.reply

It is definitely in the spirit of the story of Mel, since Tom was exploiting an intimate knowledge of the machine to achieve the impossible by using instructions in unintended ways, but always remember that Tom is not a real programmer:  Real Programmers wrote in machine code.
  Not FORTRAN.  Not RATFOR.  Not, even, assembly language.
  Machine Code.
  Raw, unadorned, inscrutable hexadecimal numbers.
  Directly.

That said, I prefer Tom's story. It's more about the joy of understanding the machine than it is about the framing of a legend.reply

title: AlphaProof Code (deepmind.google)
comments: Something seems wrong here. It wrote theorems that looked fine and the formal verification passed but the resulting code contained many, many bugs that other implementations of the same things found with ad hoc testing.The way the announcement is written, we should expect zero bugs in libsignal moving forward, and I guess time will tell whether that happens or not.reply

> they only proved narrow properties of the system.It's that, yes.They didn't prove that the code has no bugs; they proved that none of the current bugs (known or unknown) are security-breaking bugs, per their formalized security model.> First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.The generated Lean code here is just being checked against the "formal mathematical specifications of Signal's security goals", not checked for the low-level properties you might care about as a programmer, e.g. "will it ever leak memory" or "will it ever crash", etc. And in fact, the code is not even being checked for the reachability of non-security-violating protocol failure states, e.g. "could the protocol ever deadlock such that neither side can send messages any more".It's still perfectly possible for the code to have all of these problems. It's now just known that, as of the commit they did this analysis against, none of those low-level problems, as far as they exist in the codebase, can cause a security-model violation.Or, to put that another way: the system has been proven to "fail safe" in all its current failure modes, per their specific definition of safety (which is basically "keeping to the security guarantees Signal markets itself to users as having".)reply
Note that this is about Signal’s cryptographic protocol, not the Signal App or the surrounding platform OS.Proofing and securing those is the way larger attack vector and work to come.reply

I applaud them for starting with the protocol, because that can be generalized beyond any one specific implementation in principle, even if, in practice, we're somewhat limited to the official Signal apps given their centralized nature. Securing the applications themselves (perhaps starting with their implementations of the protocol, but the rest is also fair game) will inevitably be a bigger task.reply

I'm actually unclear on whether they just translated some unmentioned design specification (whitepaper, maybe?) of the Signal protocol to Lean; or whether they actually translated the official app's implementation of the protocol to Lean.I had assumed them to mean the latter, since I don't think the protocol design specification on its own would shake out into "over six million lines of Lean code." (Though if someone who knows Lean well thinks that's actually a reasonable number, please do correct me.) 6MM lines of proof code sounds more like something you get by "translating" an average-sized self-contained imperative-language library (like the protocol impl library) into a highly-rigorous prover language line-by-line, with a lot of the overhead coming from having to model imperative-language / imperative-CPU-target-abstract-machine semantics in rigorous mathematical form.Annoyingly, the wording of the article is a bit too ambiguous to say for sure either way. They just say they "generated" the Lean code; they didn't say what it was being generated from.reply

From this I think it's a given that they were talking about the implementation, not the specification> To confirm that AlphaProof Code can tell correct code from buggy code, we reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code. In both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure.Of course, there are several official pieces of software which implement the specified Signal protocol, so it's not guaranteed they verified  all of Signal's software which implements it https://github.com/signalapp/libsignalI'd be surprised if there were no security bugs in any of the code here. It's more likely that they tested the implemented logic for creating/using the cryptographic primitives, than that they actually verified there were no bugs at all in the codereply

Agreed the line can be blurry, but I want to stress that the goal of this project is NOT to push Chrome-only APIs on users.The mental model we've been using on the team is:If you hired an expert web development consultant to build X, what would they recommend as a best practice? When does it make sense to use the new API (because it provides real benefits) vs. when does it make sense to wait until it's available everywhere?To use your `fetchLater()` example, this is a case where the `fetchLater()` API legitimately solves a very real problem for people trying to build accurate analytics or telemetry features, see: https://nicj.net/beaconing-in-practice/And lots of companies actually are  already using `fetchLater()` in production now because of its increased reliability.reply
I think I can guess from corporate incentives why Chrome supports fetchLater and some others don't.reply

It's currently being added to WebKit: https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/pull/73271Regarding corporate incentives: I was involved in the design of this API, so I know the history. It was proposed many years ago as a solution to make it easier for RUM analytics providers to measure Core Web Vitals metrics that needed to account for more than just page load (e.g. layout shifts and slow interactions can happen any time, not just during page load).The RUM providers we worked with were reluctant to wait until page unload to send telemetry data because it resulted in too many lost beacons, so what they do instead is send beacons every few seconds with the most up-to-date payload.The `fetchLater()` API enables them to send just one beacon, which is good for users and also reduces their server load.reply

Why was 'fetchLater' chosen over a reliable way to trigger fetch from 'unload' or a similar event, or inversely, adding a 'sendLater' option to sendBeacon? Feels like a bolted-on API for a very specific use case, when the same thing could be built from better primitives?It's a bit sad that browsers now have two different, "standard" APIs created entirely for the purpose of user tracking, as if things weren't already bloated enough.reply
